**KYC System Design — Case Study** 

Back-end Product Management Track 

**Time required:** 3–4 hours, using AI. 

**Format:** Deliverables suitable for a CEO-level presentation. 

**Why this project** 

This case study mirrors a real problem a US FinTech must manage: end-to-end KYC handling.  Working from a synthetic KYC dataset, you will diagnose what is going wrong, design a fix,  document it to a build-ready standard, and explain how you would run it at scale. We assess  primarily how well you reason from the data, supported by informed context on US KYC. 

We will evaluate four things: 

| Structure &   communication | Answer first, then support it. Clear, MECE thinking. |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Data rigor**  | Correct denominators, honest caveats, numbers you can  stand behind. |
| **Product judgment**  | Sensible trade-offs across cost, latency, friction, and risk. |
| **Ownership**  | You can explain and defend every choice you present. |

**Note on the data:** This is a synthetic dataset. It contains no real user identifiers — only  fabricated labels that mimic the shape of typical identifiers. 

**How to approach this** 

Use AI tools freely. We expect it, and we are not testing whether you can avoid them. The rule  that matters: you must understand and be ready to defend every analytical and design decision  in the interview. We will probe your numbers, your logic, and the alternatives you rejected. “The  tool produced it” is not an answer. 

If you hit a data quirk you cannot resolve, state your assumption, handle it, and move on.  Spotting and dealing with messy data is part of the test. If you run short on time, prioritize, and  tell us what you would do with more.

**Context: US KYC for a FinTech** 

Our company must verify the identity of every user before granting access to its products.  Verification runs as a waterfall: a primary KYC provider, and, when that does not clear a user,  one or more secondary providers or checks. The current system uses these checks: 

• **Idology —** the primary identity provider. 

• **LexisNexis —** identity and SSN verification. Note that two distinct LexisNexis routes appear in the data (see the provider note below). 

• **Persona —** document and selfie verification, used in two modes: an identity mode and an SSN mode.  
• **ACRO —** an automated secondary identity check. 

• **Manual review —** a human analyst reviews cases that automation does not clear. The field overall\_kyc\_status is the final outcome that decides whether a user is verified. In  the US, an acceptable rejection rate is 5% or lower. Reconstructing, from the data, how these  checks are actually sequenced and routed today is part of Task 1\. 

**The dataset** 

You will receive sanitized data with one row per enrolled, non-deleted user, covering roughly 2.5 million users. All sensitive fields are fabricated or masked. Each provider column holds that  provider's result for the user, and a null (empty) value means the check did not run for them. 

| Column  | Meaning |
| :---- | :---- |
| Fabricated\_UID  | Fabricated unique identifier for the user. Synthetic; does not  map to any real person. |
| Fabricated\_Email  | Fabricated stand-in for the user's email. Synthetic token, not a  real address. |
| Fabricated\_SSN  | Fabricated SSN, shown only as the last four digits in the form  \*\*\*\*\*NNNN. |
| enrolled\_date  | Date the user enrolled (YYYY-MM-DD). |
| dob  | Date of birth as MM/YYYY, where available. |
| state  | US state. |
| onboarded\_bank\_partner  | Label for the partner bank through which the user was  onboarded. |
| checking\_bank\_partner  | Label for the external checking account the user connected  during onboarding. |
| kyc\_source  | The check or provider that produced the recorded outcome for  the user (see provider note below). |
| idology\_result  | Idology result: PASS, FAIL, or null. |
| lexis\_nexis\_result  | LexisNexis result: PASS, FAIL, or null. Populated by either  LexisNexis provider (see note). |
| persona\_idv\_result  | Persona identity result: PASS or null. |
| persona\_ssn\_result  | Persona SSN result: PASS or null. |
| acro\_result  | ACRO automated result: PASS, FAIL, or null. |
| manual\_review\_result  | Manual review result: PASS, FAIL, or null. |
| reviewer\_comment  | Free-text note from a manual reviewer, where one exists. |
| overall\_kyc\_status  | Final KYC outcome, stored as the literal value true (verified) or false (not verified). |

**Provider note — the two LexisNexis routes.** The kyc\_source field distinguishes two separate LexisNexis providers: ProviderA\_Lexis\_Nexis and ProviderB\_Lexis\_Nexis. Both write their   
outcome to the lexis\_nexis\_result column, but they represent different integration paths.  Part of Task 1 is to work out how each is routed and whether they behave differently. 

**A note on nulls.** Null values are stored as empty strings in the file. Persona columns only ever  take the value PASS or null — there is no FAIL value for Persona. 

**The current KYC waterfall** 

The system is understood to run roughly as follows. Confirming this against the data is part of  Task 1\. 

**Step 1 — Primary check (L1: Idology)** 

Run the primary check. If the user passes, they are verified and exit the waterfall. If they fail, log the reason (SSN error vs. non-SSN error) and route them downstream. 

**Step 2 — Split by failure type (L2 / L3)** 

• **Path A — SSN issue:** route standard users to LexisNexis and older accounts to legacy Persona-SSN. 

◦ *Crucial rule:* if these providers surface a secondary non-SSN issue, the user moves to the non-SSN track. 

• **Path B — Non-SSN issue (name / DOB / address / email):** route to ACRO or Persona IDV (document and selfie upload). 

**Step 3 — Safety net (L4: Manual review)** 

If every automated check fails, route the user to manual review for a human agent to assess.

**The tasks** 

**Task 1 — Analyze the current KYC funnel** 

Start from the data and answer one question: what is the current rejection rate, and why are  users not getting verified? 

• Reconstruct how the waterfall runs today: which checks fire, in what order, and how users route between the SSN and non-SSN paths. 

• Measure the overall non-verification rate and compare it to the 5% bar. • Diagnose the drivers. Separate genuine rejections (where verification should fail) from avoidable losses (where a verifiable user was lost to process), and quantify the largest of each. 

• Name the data caveats you ran into and how you handled them. 

***Deliverable:*** a short analysis that leads with the headline rate, breaks down the causes, and  identifies the two or three highest-leverage problems. 

**Task 2 — Design a new KYC waterfall** 

Propose a redesigned waterfall that brings non-verification to 5% or lower without weakening  genuine fraud, sanctions, or PEP controls.  
• Define the role of each provider, the routing logic, the fallbacks, and the stop conditions — where a user is hard-rejected, and why. 

• Make the cost, latency, and friction trade-offs explicit. Adding checks is not free. • Tie every change back to a specific finding from Task 1\. 

***Deliverable:*** a waterfall diagram, plus the decision logic and a short rationale. 

**Task 3 — Write the build documentation** 

Produce the documents you would hand to engineering and analytics to build your waterfall. 

• **PRD.** Goals with current baselines and targets; scope in and out; the main user flows (success, error, and escalation); and a rollout and migration plan. 

• **ARD / monitoring plan.** The metrics that prove the waterfall works — each with a definition and a threshold — plus dashboards, alerts, and what you watch during a phased rollout. 

• **Project plan.** The workstreams, owners, dependencies, sequencing, and a rollout that limits risk. 

Depth of thinking matters more than length. Concise and sharp beats long and padded. ***Deliverable:*** three documents — PRD, ARD, and project plan. 

**What to submit** 

1\. Task 1 analysis, as a presentation. 

2\. Task 2 waterfall design, as a presentation or document. 

3\. Task 3 documents: PRD, ARD, and project plan. 

Bring everything to the interview ready to walk us through and argue for your approach as the  lead product manager.
